checkpoints: The registry is an explicit static map with every import path a literal string, not a runtime lookup, because the bundler can only turn import() into a clean split point when the path is statically analyzable, and a runtime-interpolated path defeats the whole point of the registry.

Boundary placement is one Suspense per widget slot, not one boundary wrapping the whole dashboard, because a shared boundary would hold every widget hostage to the slowest chunk, showing a blank dashboard until every requested widget resolves.
Per-widget boundaries let each panel stream in independently as its own chunk lands, which is the right default when the widgets are otherwise unrelated.

Every registry entry carries a reservedHeight (or minHeight for variable content), and the Suspense fallback is a skeleton sized to that value, so zero CLS is an obligation the registry enforces rather than a convention a widget author might forget.
For genuinely variable-height content, the widget declares only a min-height and accepts a small, bounded shift instead of the large, unbounded one it would get with no reservation at all.

Every boundary sits inside an error boundary with a retry action, because import() legitimately rejects (offline, or after a redeploy invalidates the previous chunk's hash), and a bare crash there is worse than a retry button.

Admission to the registry is selective: only widgets that are heavy and off the critical path (below the fold, behind a tab, interaction-gated) belong, while a small always-visible piece of UI stays a normal static import outside the registry because the split adds a network round-trip and skeleton flash it can never pay back.
The design is verified, not assumed: the build's chunk list should show one chunk per registered widget, and Lighthouse's CLS/LCP confirm the fallback contract actually holds in the browser.

States the core justification for reaching for a worker at all: a profiled long task visibly sat on the Main track in DevTools Performance and hurt INP — the worker is a response to a measured problem, not a default choice.

Recognizes the converse case for NOT using a worker: if the work is network-bound (already yielding via await) or cheap (a few ms), the round-trip plus serialization cost outweighs the compute, so it should stay inline on the main thread.

Designs a coarse-grained API surface (e.g. one parseCsv/parseCsvToBuffer call per job) rather than a per-row RPC, because per-row calls would pay serialization plus a round-trip cost hundreds of thousands of times.
Keeps the worker free of DOM access (no document/window) — it only exchanges data, with all rendering staying on the main thread, except for the sanctioned OffscreenCanvas case.

Preserves type safety across the boundary: the worker exposes a plain object via Comlink.expose and exports its type (typeof api); the client wraps it with Comlink.wrap<T> so every call returns a Promise, honestly signaling async rather than faking a synchronous call.

Instantiates the worker in a bundler-analyzable static form (new Worker(new URL(...), { type: 'module' })) so it splits into its own chunk, and ties its lifecycle to the component — created once on mount, terminated in the unmount cleanup — rather than spinning up a fresh worker per call.
Uses Comlink.transfer for large results (zero-copy transferable buffer that detaches from the sender), reserving ordinary structured clone for small results.
The lazy boundary starts at zero height because the fallback is null or otherwise unsized, so while the chunk is in flight the page has a collapsed gap.
When the real chart (256px tall) swaps in, it pushes everything below it down, which is exactly the layout shift that CLS measures and reports as worse.
The fix is to give the Suspense fallback a skeleton with a fixed height matching the real widget (h-64 = 256px), reserving the final box up front.
With that fix, on the swap only the pixels inside the box change while the position of surrounding elements never does, so the shift contribution is 0.
For variable-height content, reserve a sensible min-height to bound the shift instead of trying to match exactly.
Verify with the Performance panel or the Web Vitals overlay while triggering the swap, confirming CLS stays at or below 0.1.
The underlying principle is that a lazy boundary without a height-matched fallback trades a bundle win for a CLS regression.
This freeze is a mount/layout problem, not a re-render problem: the browser must create, style, and lay out ~10,000 DOM nodes on first paint, a cost linear in node count and independent of React.
React.memo only skips re-renders between updates, so it cannot touch this mount-time cost.
Pagination technically cuts the node count, but it rewrites the whole UX (no continuous scroll, click pages) just to dodge a problem that belongs to the rendering layer.

The right-layer fix is windowing: the viewport only shows ~10-15 rows, so render only visible + overscan (~30 nodes), absolutely positioned by virtual offset inside a sizer div whose height equals the total so the scrollbar stays proportional.
Mount cost becomes constant in viewport size instead of data size, dropping ~2-3s to under ~50ms, with every scroll frame staying cheap because the DOM stays tiny.

Prove it by counting [data-row] nodes in the Elements panel before/after (naive ~10,000, virtualized a few dozen) and by recording the Performance panel to confirm the long Layout/Recalculate Style block disappears with FPS holding ~60 on scroll.
Memoization is a bet, not a default "wrap it to be safe" reflex — each tool trades comparison/caching overhead for skipped work, and that trade can lose.

React.memo places a shallow props-comparison gate (Object.is) in front of a child component: the bet wins only when the render work it skips is larger than the comparison cost it pays, and it loses outright when the component is cheap (comparison cost >= render cost).
It also loses when props are always a new reference every render — an inline handler or an object/array literal makes memo compare-and-lose forever, pure tax.
It loses with premature optimization — wrapping in memo before measuring, adding a deps array to maintain for no measured gain.
useMemo caches an expensive computation, like filtering/sorting a 1,000-item array, avoiding the recomputation.
useCallback keeps a handler reference stable so a memoized child's gate downstream holds — it is literally useMemo returning a function, i.e. useCallback(fn, deps) is useMemo(() => fn, deps).

The decision procedure is measurement, not guessing: record with the React DevTools Profiler and only memoize what shows significant time in the ranked view or heads a large subtree that genuinely re-renders wastefully — measure first, memoize second.
Wrong deps trade a performance smell for a correctness bug: an incorrect dependency array in useMemo/useCallback produces a stale closure, which is worse than the render it aimed to avoid.

Treat the initial chunk as a fixed budget spent only on what renders first — "lazy-load everything" ignores that a split point has a cost (a network round-trip and a skeleton flash) which must be paid back by a real saving.

A split point pays for itself only when the component is heavy — tens of KB, like a ~120 KB charting widget or a ~90 KB editor — AND off the critical path: below the fold, behind a tab, or gated behind an interaction like a button click.
Wrapping a 2 KB always-visible component in React.lazy buys nothing and makes the experience worse, not better.

manualChunks in vite.config.ts shapes how third-party vendor code is chunked: pinning a rarely-changing heavy library into its own named vendor chunk keeps that chunk's hash stable across deploys, so a returning user's browser cache serves it straight from disk and only the app code that actually changed gets re-downloaded.

The failure mode is dumping every vendor library into one giant chunk — it drags all of it back onto the critical path and invalidates the whole thing on every deploy anyway, since one shared hash means one change busts the cache for everything inside it, so vendors should be split along the same heavy/lazy lines as components, not lumped together for convenience.
In practice the highest-leverage, most common split point is at the route level — each page as its own React.lazy(() => import("./pages/...")).
Every one of these decisions gets proven by reading the npm run build chunk list and Lighthouse's Core Web Vitals, not by gut feeling about what "seems heavy."
By default, everything crossing postMessage is structured-cloned — deep-copied — so a multi-megabyte buffer pays copy time and doubles RAM on every hand-off.

A Transferable changes the deal entirely: transferring an ArrayBuffer moves ownership in constant time, zero-copy — the receiver keeps the live buffer while the sender's copy detaches to byteLength 0 — so only transfer what the sender is already done with, or slice(0) an owned copy first before transferring, exactly what the lesson's parseCsvToBuffer does before calling Comlink.transfer.

Call granularity matters just as much as the encoding choice: every cross-thread call pays serialization plus a round-trip, and because Comlink makes this boundary look exactly like a local function call, chatty designs sneak in easily — batch into one larger call instead of many small ones.
If both threads genuinely need to read in parallel at the same time, that's SharedArrayBuffer territory, which requires COOP/COEP headers.
Refuse a worker when the slowness is network-bound — an await already yields the main thread, so a worker adds no benefit.
Refuse a worker when the task is too tiny — the round-trip cost (serialization + postMessage) exceeds the compute it would save.
Refuse a worker for DOM work — DOM manipulation simply cannot move off the main thread.
The gate for the whole decision is a measured long task on the Main track, not a hunch.

The badge incrementing on every "Bump" click means ExpensiveList's props are failing React.memo's shallow Object.is comparison on every parent render: because both props are born fresh each render, memo always sees "different props" and lets the render through, now paying the comparison cost on top of the wasted render.
Root cause: ITEMS.filter(...) returns a brand-new array reference every render even when query hasn't changed.
Root cause: the inline arrow (id) => setSelectedId(id) is a new function object every render.
Fix: const filtered = useMemo(() => ITEMS.filter(...), [query]) so bumping count returns the exact same array reference.
Fix: const onSelect = useCallback((id: number) => setSelectedId(id), []) for a handler reference that never changes.
The principle from the lesson: memo only pays off when the entire reference chain above it is stable — one inline literal anywhere in that chain breaks the whole thing.

Verify with the Profiler: after the fix, repeated counter clicks show ExpensiveList "Did not render" and the badge value stays frozen, while typing into the query input still recomputes filtered and re-renders the list with the correct rows — proving useMemo caches by deps rather than freezing the data.

Every row here is position: absolute at translateY(row.start), so correctness lives entirely in the offset map; with estimateSize: () => 48 and no measureElement, the virtualizer believes every row is 48px tall regardless of actual content.

A row that wraps to three lines actually occupies roughly 3x that, but the next row's start is still computed from that wrong map — so rows paint over each other, while the hard-coded height: 48 clips the wrapped content.
The forced height also means that attaching measureElement alone, without removing it, would be pointless, since it would only measure the clipped 48px box, not the content's real height.

Fix: attach ref={virtualizer.measureElement} and data-index={row.index} on each row, and drop the fixed height — after each render the hook measures the real DOM height via ResizeObserver and corrects the offset map, so downstream start values become exact.
estimateSize keeps its role after the fix: it sizes the unrendered remainder so getTotalSize() and the scrollbar don't jump; keep it close to the average height to minimize jitter.
Verify: with long wrapped rows mid-list, there is no overlap between rows.
Verify: scrollTop doesn't snap backward while measurement corrections settle in.
Verify: scrolling to the top lands exactly at 0.
The PR's underlying instinct (pulling heavy widgets out of the initial chunk) is correct, but the execution introduces several distinct problems of varying severity.

Highest severity: `fallback={null}` on every `<Suspense>` boundary renders as zero height, so when a widget actually swaps in everything below it jumps down — a real, user-visible CLS regression; fix by giving each boundary a skeleton fallback whose height matches the real widget.

Build-time bug: `loadWidget(name)` calls `lazy(() => import(`./widgets/${name}`))` with a runtime-interpolated path that Rollup cannot statically resolve, so it either bundles every widget file into a catch-all chunk or emits a build warning, losing the clean per-widget chunking the PR claims; fix by replacing it with an explicit registry of literal, statically analyzable import paths.

Resilience gap: there is no error boundary around the lazy boundaries, so a failed chunk fetch (offline, or a stale hash after the next deploy) throws with no recovery path; fix by wrapping the lazy boundaries in an error boundary that offers retry and keeping old chunk files reachable for a deploy or two.

Lowest severity, a strategy note rather than a regression: `StatusBadge`, a small always-visible above-the-fold component, is wrapped in `React.lazy` just like the heavy widgets, which buys nothing and only adds a network round-trip and fallback flash; fix by reverting it to a static import and reserving lazy for components that are both heavy and off the critical path.
Before merging, ask for the `npm run build` chunk list before/after the change, showing exactly what left the entry chunk, rather than trusting the diff alone.
Ask for the Network panel trace confirming the lazy chunks actually fire on demand when a widget mounts, rather than eagerly on initial load.
Ask for Lighthouse LCP/CLS numbers before/after proving the split is a net win, not just a differently-shaped bundle.
